title: Thinking through a pregnancy decision
content: Poa sana kwa kuniambia. Huhitaji kuamua kila kitu sasa hivi. I can listen and help you think through what matters to you, without judging or choosing for you. If you might be pregnant, a qualified healthcare provider can confirm the pregnancy and talk through options that fit your health, timing, and local situation. You deserve confidential, respectful care and time to ask questions. Is there one part that feels most worrying right now?

title: Getting reliable information about abortion
content: Thank you for trusting me with this. I won’t judge or decide for you. Abortion options, what is medically appropriate, and what care is legally available can depend on your health, how far along a pregnancy is, and where you are. A qualified reproductive-health provider can explain confidential, evidence-based options for your circumstances. Please don’t rely on unverified sellers or take medication based only on an online chat. If you’d like, I can help you think of questions to ask a provider or how to find a trusted service. If you’re in Kenya, local law and services need to be confirmed directly with a qualified provider; I can’t give a legal eligibility decision.

source.title: WHO — Abortion care guideline

title: Supporting someone without pressure
content: A good first step is to listen and ask what kind of support they want. You might say, “I’m here with you. I won’t pressure you. What would feel helpful right now?” Respect their privacy, avoid pushing your own choice, and offer practical support—like helping them contact a qualified provider or going with them if they ask. If they seem unsafe or are being coerced, ask privately what would help them feel safer and connect them with trusted, local support.

source.title: WHO — Abortion care guideline
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: When someone is pressuring you
content: I’m sorry you’re facing pressure. A pregnancy decision should be yours, made freely and with support—not because someone is threatening or forcing you. If it feels safe, consider talking privately with a trusted person or a qualified health worker. Use a device or account that feels safe if someone may check your messages. If you’re in immediate danger, contact local emergency services or go somewhere safer and seek urgent help. You don’t have to share names or identifying details with me.

title: When to get urgent medical help
content: Please seek urgent in-person medical care now if you have very heavy bleeding, severe or worsening pain, fainting, a high fever, or feel seriously unwell—especially during pregnancy or after a pregnancy-related treatment. Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest health facility. Don’t wait for an online reply if symptoms feel severe. I can’t diagnose what is causing them.

title: What Nia can help with
content: I’m Nia, a supportive information guide—not a doctor, therapist, lawyer, or emergency service. I can share general information from a small local guide, help you prepare questions for a qualified provider, or listen while you sort through what matters to you. I can’t diagnose, prescribe, confirm what is legal for your specific case, or replace confidential care. This demo does not save your chat history in a database, but don’t share names, phone numbers, or details you want to keep private. Voice recognition and speech playback may be handled by your browser or device.

title: Sexual health and wellbeing
content: Sexual health is part of overall wellbeing. It can include physical health, emotional wellbeing, relationships, consent, and access to respectful information and care. You can ask about contraception, periods, pregnancy, infections, or relationships here. I can share general information, but I can’t diagnose or replace a healthcare professional. What would you like to know?

source.title: WHO — Sexual health
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: Contraception options
phrases: what contraception options can i use
content: There are several ways to prevent pregnancy, including condoms, pills, injections, implants, and intrauterine devices. They differ in how they are used, possible side effects, how long they last, and whether they also reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections. The best fit depends on your health, preferences, and access. A qualified provider or pharmacist can explain locally available options and answer personal medical questions. Condoms are the method in this list that also helps reduce STI transmission when used correctly and consistently.

source.title: WHO — Family planning/contraception methods
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: Emergency contraception
content: If contraception failed or sex happened without contraception and you want to avoid pregnancy, contact a qualified pharmacist or health service as soon as you can to ask about emergency contraception. Some options are time-sensitive, and the right option depends on your circumstances and what is available locally. Emergency contraception does not end an established pregnancy and does not protect against STIs. A pharmacist or clinician can explain safe use for you; don’t rely on an unverified product or online dosing advice.

source.title: WHO — Emergency contraception
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: Pregnancy concern after sex
phrases: had sex last week and might be pregnant
not sure if she got pregnant
not sure if they got pregnant
had unprotected sex and worried about pregnancy
content: I can’t tell from a chat whether pregnancy happened; the chance depends on what contraception was used and other details. If sex was without contraception or a method failed and it was within the last 5 days, contact a pharmacist or health service as soon as possible to ask about emergency contraception—WHO says it works best the sooner it is used. Since “last week” can mean different numbers of days, tell them the exact day. For a pregnancy test, the NHS advises testing from the first day of a missed period, or at least 21 days after unprotected sex if you do not know when your period is due. Follow the test instructions; if a result is negative but your period still does not come, repeat it after a few days or contact a health professional. If you share whether contraception was used and when the next period is due, I can help you find the relevant general information.

title: STI testing and prevention
content: Many sexually transmitted infections (STIs) can have no noticeable symptoms, so testing is the reliable way to know your status. A clinic or qualified health worker can advise which tests are appropriate, when to test, and whether a partner should also be tested. Using condoms correctly and consistently can lower the risk of many STIs. If you think you may have been exposed, contact a health service for confidential advice rather than waiting for symptoms. This chat cannot diagnose an STI.

source.title: WHO — Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: Possible STI symptoms
content: Unusual discharge, sores, a rash, itching, or pain when urinating can have different causes, including an STI, and some STIs cause no symptoms at all. Please arrange a confidential assessment and testing with a qualified health worker. Until you get advice, consider avoiding sex or using condoms to lower the chance of passing an infection. Don’t use leftover antibiotics or treatments recommended online. Seek urgent care for severe pain, fever, or feeling seriously unwell.

source.title: WHO — Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: Condoms and safer sex
content: Condoms can help reduce the risk of pregnancy and many sexually transmitted infections when used correctly and consistently. Use a new condom for each sex act, check the package and expiry date, and follow its instructions. If a condom breaks or slips, a pharmacist or health service can discuss time-sensitive pregnancy prevention and STI advice. Condoms do not remove all risk, and this general information is not a substitute for a clinician’s advice about your situation.

source.title: WHO — Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: Consent and personal boundaries
phrases: i do not want to have sex
content: Consent means freely choosing to take part. It should be clear, ongoing, and can be changed or withdrawn at any time. Being in a relationship or having agreed before does not mean you have agreed now. Pressure, threats, fear, or being unable to choose freely are not consent. If you feel unsafe, consider contacting someone you trust or a local support service from a safe device. If you are in immediate danger, seek urgent local help. You do not have to share identifying details here.

source.title: WHO — Sexual health
source.review_status: Starter summary — safeguarding review required

title: When and how to check for pregnancy
phrases: when to take a pregnancy test
content: A home pregnancy test can help check for pregnancy. Follow the instructions that come with the test and ask a pharmacist or health worker if you are unsure how to use or interpret it. If a result is negative but your period still does not come, or the result is unclear, repeat testing according to the product instructions or contact a qualified provider. A clinician can confirm a result and discuss next steps without pressure. Severe pain, fainting, or heavy bleeding needs urgent in-person care.

source.title: NHS — Doing a pregnancy test
source.review_status: Starter summary — check local availability and review

title: Periods and menstrual cycles
phrases: how does my menstrual cycle work
content: Menstrual cycles can vary between people and may change over time. Stress, illness, changes in routine, pregnancy, and other health factors can affect bleeding patterns. A late or missed period does not by itself confirm pregnancy; consider a pregnancy test if pregnancy is possible. Contact a qualified health worker if a change worries you, bleeding is unusually heavy, pain is severe, or periods stop unexpectedly. Nia cannot diagnose the cause of a cycle change.

source.title: NHS — Periods
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: Vaginal health and discharge
content: Vaginal discharge can change during the menstrual cycle, but a new or persistent change in smell, colour, amount, or texture—or itching, soreness, pain, or bleeding—can need assessment. These symptoms can have several causes, so a qualified health worker can test and advise. Avoid putting soaps, scented products, or unprescribed treatments inside the vagina. Seek urgent care if you have severe pain, fever, or feel seriously unwell.

source.title: NHS — Vaginal discharge

title: If you may have been exposed to HIV
phrases: may have been exposed to hiv
condom broke with hiv positive partner
content: If you think you may have had a recent exposure to HIV, contact an emergency department, clinic, or qualified health worker urgently and explain when the exposure happened. A clinician can assess whether post-exposure prevention is appropriate; it is time-sensitive. I can’t determine your risk or prescribe treatment here. Ask about confidential HIV testing and other sexual-health support as well.

title: Pain or discomfort during sex
content: Pain or bleeding during or after sex can have different causes and deserves respectful attention. You do not have to continue an activity that hurts or that you do not want. If the discomfort repeats, is new, or worries you, speak with a qualified health worker who can assess possible causes. Seek urgent care for severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, or feeling seriously unwell. This chat cannot diagnose the cause.

source.title: WHO — Sexual health

title: Preparing to talk with a health provider
phrases: what should i ask my doctor
how to talk to a health provider
questions for a reproductive health clinic
i am nervous to see a doctor
content: It can help to write down what you want to ask, when symptoms or concerns began, any medicines you take, and what matters most to you. You can ask what information is confidential, what choices are available, possible benefits and risks, costs, and where to get follow-up care. You may ask to speak without a partner or family member present, or bring a trusted person if you want. You do not have to agree to something you do not understand; ask the provider to explain it in a way that works for you.

source.title: WHO — Sexual health
source.review_status: Starter summary — local service review required

title: Fertility and trying to become pregnant
phrases: why am i not getting pregnant
content: Fertility depends on many factors and can involve either or both partners. If you have concerns, a qualified healthcare provider can discuss your health history, any medicines, and what assessment may be helpful. Be cautious of products or online promises that claim to guarantee pregnancy. If you are planning a pregnancy, a clinician can offer personalized pre-pregnancy health advice. I can share general information but can’t predict an individual’s fertility.

source.title: WHO — Infertility

title: Menopause and changing periods
content: Menopause is a natural life stage when menstrual periods stop, and the transition can bring changes such as hot flushes, sleep changes, or mood changes. Experiences vary, and other health conditions can cause similar symptoms. A qualified provider can help discuss symptom support and check concerns such as bleeding after periods have stopped. If symptoms affect daily life, you deserve care and options to discuss.

source.title: WHO — Menopause
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: Puberty and body changes
content: Puberty brings physical and emotional changes, and the timing and pace are different for everyone. Questions about periods, body changes, feelings, or relationships are normal to ask. A trusted adult or qualified health worker can offer support; you can ask to speak privately and ask what will remain confidential. If someone is pressuring or hurting you, seek help from a safe trusted adult or local support service. I can share general information but cannot replace care.

source.title: WHO — Adolescent health

title: HIV testing and prevention
phrases: how do i get tested for hiv
content: HIV testing is the way to know your status, and a qualified health service can explain available tests, confidentiality, prevention, and treatment. Effective treatment helps people living with HIV stay healthy. If you think a recent exposure may have occurred, seek urgent medical advice because post-exposure prevention is time-sensitive. Nia cannot assess your individual risk or interpret a test result; a trained health worker can help.

source.title: WHO — HIV and AIDS
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: HPV vaccination and cervical screening
content: HPV is a common virus; some types can cause health problems, including cervical cancer. HPV vaccination and cervical screening can help prevent disease, but recommendations and availability depend on age and local health guidance. A qualified provider can tell you which vaccine or screening schedule applies to you and where to access it. Screening is still important for eligible people who have been vaccinated. This chat cannot assess your personal risk or test results.

source.title: WHO — Human papillomavirus (HPV) and cervical cancer

title: Getting care during pregnancy
content: If you are pregnant, a qualified health worker or midwife can discuss check-ups, your health, medicines, and questions throughout pregnancy. Starting care early when possible can help you understand available support and what to expect. You can ask what services are confidential and what costs or options are available locally. Seek urgent in-person care for severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, or feeling seriously unwell. This chat cannot monitor a pregnancy or replace antenatal care.

source.title: WHO — Maternal health
source.review_status: Starter summary — local clinical review required

title: Support after pregnancy loss
content: I’m sorry you’re worried or going through this. Bleeding or pain during pregnancy can have different causes and needs assessment; it is not possible to confirm a miscarriage through chat. Please contact a qualified health service for advice. Seek urgent care now for heavy bleeding, severe pain, fainting, or feeling seriously unwell. Pregnancy loss can also bring grief and many feelings—support from someone you trust or a trained counsellor may help.

title: Changes in erection or sexual function
content: Changes in erections, desire, or other parts of sexual function are common reasons to seek care, and they can have physical, emotional, or medicine-related causes. A qualified healthcare provider can discuss what is happening and whether an assessment is appropriate. Avoid unverified supplements or prescription medicines bought without a clinician’s advice. Sudden severe pain or injury needs urgent medical attention.

title: Sexual orientation, identity, and respectful care
content: It is okay to have questions about attraction, identity, or relationships, and you do not have to label yourself or share anything before you are ready. You deserve respectful, non-discriminatory care. If you choose to talk with someone, consider whether they are trustworthy and whether it feels safe to share. A qualified, affirming health professional or support organization may be able to help with personal questions and local resources.
